response.text:
“Does It Look Sequential?” (RecSys 2024) evaluates GRU4Rec and SASRec by shuffling inference histories while keeping holdout targets fixed, using the same trained checkpoint. It measures HR@10/NDCG@10 degradation and top-10 Jaccard overlap; several datasets show weak sensitivity. Crucially, excluding the holdout target from shuffling does **not** preserve the latest input interaction. Its shuffle therefore combines disruption of the last-item signal with disruption of earlier order, and cannot isolate longer-context dependence. [Paper](https://arxiv.org/html/2408.12008v1)

For the proposed GRU4Rec diagnosis, use paired validation-only controls on the same checkpoint: original history; last-item-only input; shuffle earlier interactions while fixing the last input item; and delete equal numbers of recent versus oldest interactions while preserving that last item in both conditions. Repack and left-pad consistently, retaining identical users, targets and candidate sets. These are proposed diagnostic extensions, not the paper’s reported protocol. A drop under last-preserving shuffling indicates sensitivity to earlier order; a larger drop from recent-context deletion than oldest deletion suggests reliance on nearby context beyond the last item. Last-item-only similarity instead suggests that most predictive value comes from the latest interaction, although truncation also changes the input distribution. Complement HR@10 changes with recommendation-list overlap: accuracy can remain stable while recommendations change. The broader distinction between last-item evidence, accumulated earlier-item evidence and joint sequence modelling is articulated in [Spotify’s benchmark analysis](https://research.atspotify.com/2026/10/do-sequential-recommendation-benchmarks-require-higher-order-sequence-modelling).
